items.prompt: What makes a wave glow blue as it breaks at night?

options.label: Tiny drifting organisms lighting up
options.feedback: Disturbance sets off a flash in each one.

options.label: Moonlight reflecting off the foam
options.feedback: It happens on moonless nights too.

options.label: Minerals in the sand catching light
options.feedback: The glow appears far from any shore as well.

options.label: Electricity building up in the water
options.feedback: Sea water carries no such charge.

items.ok_line: The water is not glowing. Millions of small things in it are.
items.ko_line: It only appears where the water is stirred. What could respond to being disturbed?
items.exp_title: The sea does not glow — its passengers do
items.exp_text: Blue light in a breaking wave comes from dinoflagellates, single-celled drifters that flash when the water around them is sheared. Each flash lasts a fraction of a second, and it takes many millions to light a wave. Drag a hand through the water and it leaves a glowing trail; walk on wet sand and each footprint lights up for a moment.

items.prompt: What sets off the flash of a glowing plankton cell?

options.label: Being pushed or squeezed by moving water
options.feedback: The cell detects the force on its own wall.

options.label: Sunlight stored earlier in the day
options.feedback: Nothing is stored; the flash is made on demand.

options.label: Contact with another cell
options.feedback: It flashes alone in open water.

options.label: A drop in the water temperature
options.feedback: Temperature changes far too slowly.

items.ok_line: It is a response to being handled, and it is nearly instant.
items.ko_line: Still water stays dark. Stir it and it lights. What did the stirring do?
items.exp_text: The cell senses the shearing force of moving water against its wall, and within about twenty thousandths of a second an electrical signal crosses it and triggers the reaction. This is far faster than most single-celled behaviour. Because the trigger is mechanical, the display maps the movement exactly — a boat's wake, a fish's turn, or a swimmer's arm all draw themselves in light.

items.prompt: Why would a single-celled drifter flash when disturbed?

options.label: It exposes whatever is eating it
options.feedback: The light draws a larger hunter to the attacker.

options.label: It blinds its attacker instantly
options.feedback: A single cell's flash is far too weak for that.

options.label: It warns other cells to flee
options.feedback: A drifter cannot swim away from anything.

options.label: It makes the cell taste unpleasant
options.feedback: Light has no taste.

items.ok_line: It cannot fight or flee, so it calls the police.
items.ko_line: A cell too small to defend itself lights up its own attacker. Who benefits from seeing that?
items.exp_text: A drifting cell can neither flee nor fight, but it can make its attacker conspicuous. A small crustacean grazing on glowing plankton lights up and becomes an easy target for a fish. Tank experiments confirm it: grazers are caught far more often when their food glows, and they learn to avoid feeding on it. The cell does not save itself, but its neighbours are left alone.

options.label: Plankton multiplying to enormous numbers
options.feedback: So dense that the water changes colour.

options.label: Sand stirred up by a strong current
options.feedback: Sediment makes water brown, and it does not glow.

options.label: The tide at sunset
options.feedback: The colour has nothing to do with the hour.

options.label: Iron leaking from rocks on the shore
options.feedback: Rust does not spread across open water.

items.ok_line: Red or brown by day, and often brilliantly blue by night.
items.ko_line: Something living is multiplying fast enough to stain the sea.
items.exp_title: Brown by day, blue by night
items.exp_text: When conditions suit them, dinoflagellates multiply until there are millions in a litre and the water turns rust-red or brown in daylight. If the species happens to be a glowing one, the same water lights up spectacularly after dark. Many blooms are harmful for a separate reason: some species produce toxins that accumulate in shellfish, which is why harvesting is banned during them.

options.label: A bay where glowing plankton stay trapped
options.feedback: A narrow mouth keeps them from washing out.

options.label: A bay lit by lamps along the shore
options.feedback: Artificial light spoils the effect entirely.

options.label: A bay where the seabed itself glows
options.feedback: The glow is in the water, not the bottom.

options.label: A bay that glows only after a storm
options.feedback: The best ones glow nearly every night.

items.ok_line: The shape of the bay is what keeps the population there.
items.ko_line: These bays glow almost every night of the year. Something is holding the plankton in place.
items.exp_title: Held in by the shape of the shore
items.exp_text: A handful of bays glow nearly every night because a narrow entrance stops the water flushing out, while mangroves along the shore shed nutrients that feed the plankton. Mosquito Bay in Puerto Rico is the brightest measured anywhere. They are fragile: dredging the entrance, cutting the mangroves or adding shoreline lighting can end the phenomenon, and several bays have gone dark and never recovered.

items.prompt: How did glowing plankton once betray ships at sea?

options.label: A submarine left a glowing wake
options.feedback: The disturbed water lit its track from above.

options.label: They corroded the metal hulls
options.feedback: Plankton do not attack steel.

options.label: They jammed the radio signals
options.feedback: Living cells produce no radio interference.

options.label: They blocked the engine intakes
options.feedback: They are far too small to clog anything.

items.ok_line: A vessel meant to be invisible, drawing its own path in light.
items.ko_line: These organisms flash when water is disturbed. What passes through water trying not to be seen?
items.exp_title: The wake that gave the game away
items.exp_text: Anything moving through plankton-rich water sets off a glow along its track, and a submerged submarine can leave a luminous trail visible from an aircraft. Both world wars produced reports of vessels detected this way, and navies have studied the effect seriously since. The same phenomenon reveals shoals of fish and swimming dolphins, each drawing itself in a moving outline of light.

items.prompt: Are glowing plankton animals or plants?

options.label: Neither — they are a group of their own
options.feedback: Single cells that are neither animal nor plant.

options.label: They are very small animals
options.feedback: Many of them photosynthesise, which no animal does.

options.label: They are floating plants
options.feedback: Many hunt and eat other cells, which no plant does.

options.label: They are a kind of bacteria
options.feedback: Their cells have a nucleus; bacteria have none.

items.ok_line: They refuse both boxes, and some do both jobs at once.
items.ko_line: Some of them photosynthesise like a plant and eat like an animal. Which box fits?
items.exp_title: Neither one thing nor the other
items.exp_text: Dinoflagellates belong to a group that is neither animal, plant nor fungus. Many carry chloroplasts and feed on sunlight; many others hunt and swallow other cells; and a number do both, depending on what is available. They swim with two whip-like tails set at right angles, one wrapped in a groove around the body, which makes them spin as they go — hence the name.

items.prompt: Why do glowing plankton flash mostly at night?

options.label: An internal clock silences them by day
options.feedback: The response is suppressed even in constant darkness.

options.label: Daylight physically prevents the flash
options.feedback: The cell can flash by day; it simply does not.

options.label: They sink too deep during the day
options.feedback: The rhythm holds in a tank at fixed depth.

options.label: There is nothing to disturb them by day
options.feedback: Waves break all day long.

items.ok_line: A clock inside the cell, and it keeps running in the dark.
items.ko_line: Kept in permanent darkness they still fall quiet at the right hours. What does that show?
items.exp_title: A clock in a single cell
items.exp_text: The flash response is under circadian control: it is strong at night and suppressed by day, and the rhythm continues for weeks in constant dim light, drifting only slowly. That is what proves the clock is internal rather than a reaction to daylight. These single cells became one of the classic laboratory subjects for studying biological clocks, precisely because the flash is so easy to measure.

items.prompt: Where is the light produced inside one of these cells?

options.label: In tiny compartments in the cell wall
options.feedback: Small sacs that fire when the signal reaches them.

options.label: Throughout the whole cell at once
options.feedback: The light comes from specific structures.

options.label: On the surface, in a thin film
options.feedback: The machinery is inside, not on the skin.

options.label: In the two swimming tails
options.feedback: The tails move the cell; they make no light.

items.ok_line: Small dedicated sacs, arranged around the edge of the cell.
items.ko_line: The flash is fast and precise, so the machinery must be gathered somewhere specific.
items.exp_text: The reaction is packed into tiny compartments called scintillons, spaced around the inside of the cell wall, each holding the fuel and the enzyme ready to fire. When the electrical signal from a disturbance sweeps past, the compartment becomes briefly acidic and the reaction runs. Keeping everything separated until the moment it is needed is what makes such a fast, brief flash possible in a single cell.

items.prompt: What is the best way to see glowing plankton?

options.label: A dark moonless night, away from lights
options.feedback: And twenty minutes with no torch at all.

options.label: A bright full moon over calm water
options.feedback: Moonlight washes the effect out completely.

options.label: Midday, from a high cliff
options.feedback: Daylight overwhelms it entirely.

options.label: Under a strong lamp on the shore
options.feedback: Any nearby light ruins it.

items.ok_line: No moon, no torch, no phone — and patience.
items.ko_line: The glow is faint. Anything brighter than it will hide it.
items.exp_text: The glow is faint enough that a full moon, a streetlamp or a single glance at a phone screen will hide it. The best conditions are a moonless night, warm water in late summer, no artificial light within sight, and twenty to thirty minutes for the eyes to adjust. Then stir the water: the flash follows the movement, and the display is made by the person watching it.
